summary: Deep technical session comparing kernel selection and runtime behavior between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on customer GPU fleet. Covered CUDA graphs, KV cache implications, batching tradeoffs, quantization constraints, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed on benchmark plan and next steps.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Today Ethan and Carlos from Redwood will walk through GPU runtime profiling, kernel selection, and a head-to-head of TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM. We planned ~70 minutes. Sarah, Priya, Tom are you good?
[00:12] Dr. Sarah Kim: Yup, thanks. We're particularly interested in tail latency for chat workloads and cost per token for high throughput reranking.
[00:20] Ethan: Great. Quick agenda: we'll show profiling outputs (CUDA graphs, kernel timelines), discuss kernel selection heuristics, then compare TRT-LLM vs vLLM on short and long seq len profiles, plus quantization notes.
[00:35] Tom: Also want to confirm networking: these runs will be in our VPC on prem-ish cluster, not public cloud, driver versions locked.
[00:43] Maya: Correct — we know you care about VPC / on-prem constraints and KMS. We'll keep that in mind.
[00:52] Ethan: Jumping in — first slide. Kernel selection: runtime picks different fused kernels depending on model size, attention pattern, seqlen. For example TRT-LLM will pick a fused FMA+softmax kernel for certain attention block sizes; vLLM (and CPU-backed runtimes) rely more on separate CUDA kernels and explicit KV cache copies.
[01:18] Ethan: Here's a profiling trace from a 2k-token profile. You can see the enqueue pattern, then big kernel A (tenser RT name in the trace because of auto mapping), then a long memcpy — that's KV cache spill for long context.
[01:34] Dr. Sarah Kim: That memcpy — is that host-device or device-to-device?
[01:37] Ethan: In this trace it's device-to-device but through a staging buffer because of our batching layer. We sometimes see accidental host syncs when batching logic isn't pinned correctly — that is what kills tail latency.
[01:50] Priya: We saw similar behavior when running vllm; spikes around 300-400ms.
[01:55] Ethan: Exactly. vLLM has a different caching strategy — it keeps KV on device but the codepaths for certain attention patterns cause extra memmoves. TRT-LLM on the other hand fuses more ops and can avoid some copies, but only if kernel selection matches your seqlen and head dims.
[02:13] Carlos: Quick note on CUDA graphs: capturing graphs can remove a lot of launch overhead, especially for stable micro-batches. But graphs are brittle across shapes and require a graph capture phase — if your runtime switches graph shapes mid-run (different seq lens), you pay capture overhead or must maintain multiple graphs.
[02:32] Tom: How much gain are we talking about?
[02:35] Ethan: In our tests with 8xA100 and a 2k seqlen chat style workload, enabling focused CUDA graphs gave a 15-25% token throughput improvement and lowered p95 latency by ~10-15%, provided the workload shape stayed consistent. When shapes vary, benefit is reduced because you amortize multiple captures.
[02:53] Dr. Sarah Kim: What about quantization? We're looking at int8 to reduce cost. How compatible is that with TRT-LLM vs vLLM?
[02:59] Ethan: TRT-LLM has mature int8 support in TensorRT but requires calibration or QAT for best results; it benefits a lot from per-channel quant. vLLM has experimental quant pipelines and tends to use 4-bit/LLM.int8 approximations in open implementations. For production-grade int8 with low regressions, TRT-LLM currently has the edge, but it depends on your model family and perf/quality tradeoff.
[03:20] Maya: Sarah, you mentioned reranking and chat. Which is higher priority?
[03:24] Dr. Sarah Kim: Both. Reranking is very cost-sensitive; chat needs predictable latency. We may want a hybrid: quantized model for reranking and a slightly higher-precision for chat.
[03:32] Ethan: That's a good use case for smart routing — route rerank to quantized TRT instances and chat to FP16 TRT or vLLM depending on latency. Redwood's runtime can do that at the request layer.
[03:44] [04:00] Ethan: Showed kernel timeline screenshot — you can see kernels labeled as "trt_fused_attn" then a block labeled "memcpy D2D" and several small launches.
[04:13] Tom: Some of our infra folks noted strange context resets that forced kernel reinitialization — could that be driver mismatch?
[04:20] Carlos: Yes, driver/toolkit mismatches are a common source. Also dynamic mixed precision flags and cuBLAS fallback can cause unexpected kernel choices. We recommend pinned CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT versions across nodes and checking for cuBLASLt fallback to non-fused kernels.
[04:36] Dr. Sarah Kim: When you compared TRT-LLM vs vLLM what hardware did you run on?
[04:40] Ethan: 8xA100 80GB, NVIDIA driver 535.xx, CUDA 12.x, TensorRT 8.9 in the TRT experiment. vLLM runs used PyTorch 2.1 + the vLLM runtime compiled against the same CUDA. We attempted to keep env identical, but small differences in cuBLAS / cublasLt selection exist.
[04:59] Ethan: Results: for seq len 128 (high throughput), vLLM and TRT-LLM are within 5-10% in tokens/sec; for seq len 1024/2048 TRT-LLM pulls ahead 20-40% when fused kernels are applicable. Tail latencies improved more with TRT when CUDA graphs enabled and batching stable.
[05:25] Priya: Any gotchas with checkpoint formats? We run HF checkpoints.
[05:30] Ethan: Good question. TRT-LLM prefers ONNX or TRT-serialized engines; conversion from HF can introduce ops mismatch or suboptimal graph lowering. vLLM works directly with HF weights (and supports sharded checkpoints). Conversion step should be part of the benchmark — sometimes conversion produces suboptimal kernel shapes.
[05:48] Dr. Sarah Kim: Can you show an example of a bad kernel choice?
[05:51] Ethan: Yep — here's a trace where attention was split into two kernels because head_dim wasn't divisible by the preferred tile size; that produced 2x kernel launches and extra memops.
[06:04] [06:15] Tom: For on-prem VPC, are there security considerations with CUDA graphs or TRT engines?
[06:20] Carlos: The engines themselves are binary artifacts; you should treat them as code — store them in your artifact registry, sign them if needed, and control access. CUDA graphs don't expose data but the capture process could write temporary buffers — ensure temp directories and permissions are locked down.
[06:36] Dr. Sarah Kim: About observability: what should we capture during our benchmark?
[06:40] Carlos: NVTX ranges in the code, CUDA Graph graphs, cupti timeline, kernel occupancy, and runtime logs (TensorRT engine info). Also Redwood's tracing will capture per-request token timing and batching decisions — we can overlay those with the low-level traces.
[06:53] Ethan: We'll share a lightweight collector script that runs nsys / nvprof equivalently and pushes a couple of artifacts.
[07:00] [07:25] Priya: If we want to enable CUDA graphs in production, how many graph variants do you expect?
[07:30] Ethan: Depends on workload shape diversity. For chat + rerank, we'd expect maybe 3-6 graphs: short chat, long chat, rerank small batch, rerank large batch. Each extra graph increases memory footprint (engine + graph) and management complexity.
[07:45] Dr. Sarah Kim: Any quick wins to reduce KV cache memcopies?
[07:48] Ethan: Avoid unnecessary device-host roundtrips; use device-resident batching and pin memory for host staging. Also ensure the runtime keeps KV cache in contiguous buffers to enable cuMemcpyAsync D2D and avoid small fragmented copies.
[08:03] Tom: We have a question: we saw unexpected p99 spikes only when concurrency changed from 8 to 16. Thoughts?
[08:09] Carlos: Likely queueing and batching interactions. When concurrency increases, batch coalescing logic can create larger batch sizes and trigger different kernel shapes; also memory pressure can cause occasional GPU OOMs and reinitialization — watch for driver logs.
[08:24] Ethan: We'll instrument batch size distributions and correlate with kernel shapes.
[08:30] [08:45] Ethan: Demo time — showing two side-by-side traces: TRT with CUDA graphs vs vLLM baseline. You can see smoother timeline on TRT with graphs; vLLM has more small launches and jitter.
[09:02] Dr. Sarah Kim: How reproducible are these numbers across multiple runs?
[09:06] Ethan: We run 10-ish runs and report median and p95/p99. TRT graphs help reduce variance but conversion or capture flakiness can add noise. Reproducibility is better when the stack is pinned.
[09:18] Maya: Recap and proposed pilot: Redwood SE runs TRT-LLM and vLLM benchmarks on your 8xA100 test cluster across two profiles (chat short=128, chat long=1024+ and rerank small batch). We'll collect CUDA graphs, kernel timelines, and observe tail latencies.
[09:34] Dr. Sarah Kim: That sounds good. What access do you need?
[09:37] Priya: We'll provision a test VPC with SSH keys and a shared S3 bucket for logs.
[09:41] Maya: Perfect. Ethan, Carlos — you got the plan?
[09:44] Ethan: Yep — we'll start once Priya shares access. We'll aim to have preliminary results by next Friday.
[09:50] Tom: One last thing — any advice on TRT engine caching and invalidation?
[09:54] Carlos: Keep engine versioning tied to model version and graph shape; store engine metadata (CUDA driver, TensorRT version, model hash) so you can detect invalidation and avoid silent mismatches.
[10:06] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the benchmark sheet, the collector scripts, and a proposed pilot pricing.
[10:12] Dr. Sarah Kim: Thanks, very useful.
[10:15] Ethan: Thanks all.

Notes: transcript contains occasional auto-transcription errors (e.g., "tenser RT" for TensorRT). Referenced artifacts: benchmark_spreadsheet.xlsx (link shared), cuda_graphs_examples.tar.gz (link), trt_tuning_guide.pdf (link).
